blogs.content:
Release: datasette-apps 0.3a0

 Datasette Apps adds support for hosting and editing custom HTML applications inside of Datasette.

 These can be created by hand, but it's easier to create them using LLMs via Datasette Agent . This release improves that integration:

 Apps can now be tagged in Datasette Agent chat messages by typing # , which autocompletes from the apps the user has permission to view.

 New app_add_stored_queries() and app_remove_stored_queries() tools let the agent manage which stored queries an app is allowed to call. Granting a write query requires approval from the user first.

 app_create() now checks that each requested stored query exists and that the user can view it, and asks the user to approve any write queries before the app is created.

 The "View app" buttons shown by the agent tools, and the links on # app references, now open the app full screen in the Datasette Agent panel.

 Tags: datasette , datasette-agent , datasette-apps

Release: datasette-agent 0.5a0

 This is a significant release of Datasette Agent . The most notable new feature is called the panel - it lets the agent chat open and then sit next to pages from Datasette, for example a table or query page.

 When combined with datasette-apps this means you can prompt a database-backed app into existence and then modify it from the chat that sits next to that app.

 You can try it by signing in with your GitHub account to agent.datasette.io .

blogs.name: Stratechery by Ben Thompson
blogs.title: AI on the Ballot
blogs.author: Ben Thompson
blogs.description:
Listen to this post: Log in to listen

From Bloomberg this morning at 2 a.m. Central:

Democrats won…
blogs.content:
Listen to this post :

 Log in to listen

 From Bloomberg this morning at 2 a.m. Central:

 Democrats won control of both chambers of the US Congress in a midterm election landslide that amounted to a rejection of President Donald Trump following widespread voter discontent with the economy and the war in Iran. Across the country, Democrats scored victories in GOP strongholds, flipping at least seven Senate seats and winning House races in districts Republicans easily carried in 2024. Several news organizations projected that Democrats would win the House, while Decision Desk HQ projected they took the Senate.

 I have no doubt that Iran and the economy played significant roles in this election; what stood out to me, however, was very much Stratechery fodder. Specifically, I watch a lot of sports, and particularly this fall, watched a lot of baseball. My Milwaukee Brewers — excuse me, my World Champion Milwaukee Brewers — demanded my full attention, which also meant I saw a lot of campaign ads, and by far the most common topic, at least here in Wisconsin, was data centers. Moreover, it was never entirely clear which way it cut politically: both parties were anti-data center, accusing their opponent of being the opposite.

 Meanwhile in Texas, from Yahoo Finance :

 A strong showing by Democrats in Texas swept Gina Hinojosa into office as the state’s first Democratic governor since 1990 in a contest closely watched by Big Tech companies. The state is considered a bellwether for government restrictions on AI data centers…Hinojosa, Texas’ first Latina governor, has pledged to impose a moratorium on data center construction in Texas, which accounts for more than 25% of planned US capacity by 2030.

 Republican incumbent Greg Abbott, I would note, already declared a moratorium on new data-center permits in September; that’s how much of a hot-button issue this is, including in the state that is the biggest opportunity and beneficiary of the data center buildout. So yeah, this is a Stratechery topic of concern.

 The Data Center Veto

 Earlier this year, while writing about data center opposition , I said:

 There really wasn’t widespread opposition to data centers when they were being built for the Internet generally; indeed, local governments would compete for them, eager for the economic benefits that came during their construction and the long-term tax benefits once they were operational. In other words, it seems pretty clear that the current wave of opposition can’t be divorced from AI — you know, the technology that in the best case scenario is going to take everyone’s jobs, and in the worst case scenario end the human race.

 I do not, I don’t think, need to explain to you why this is not a very compelling message, and, in the very long run, I do think that humans will have economic value . At the same time, it’s hard to explain the huge amount of investment that is going into AI, not just at the model level but also in terms of data centers, without admitting that a big part of the thesis is that AI can not just increase the top line for companies, but also increase the bottom line — i.e. replace the jobs of some number of humans. Again, I’m generally an optimist here, but this already happened with the first wave of IT .

 That leads to an interesting contrast to globalization: when companies were closing down American factories and laying off workers and moving operations to China, none of the affected towns or workers had a say. They just suddenly no longer had a job, and a huge number of cities across the Rust Belt no longer had a reason to exist. People simply had to move, or worse, retreat to things like alcohol or drugs. AI, however, is the opposite: building data centers requires permission, which is to say that people actually have a say. Again, I am not at all saying that these people are well informed about data centers, or about the economic impact on their communities, much less the economic impact of AI generally; what I am noting is that people who didn’t have a say in globalization are suddenly finding they do have a say about AI, and it’s not a surprise they are expressing their disapproval by blocking data centers.

 That message was loud and clear last spring; now it is deafening, and it’s tempting to say that tech, particularly the frontier labs, have no one to blame but themselves. In fact, however, some of the biggest culprits may, in the long run, be some of the biggest beneficiaries of the anti-data center wave.

 My thesis — driven not just by national results and the Texas governorship, but also the fact that, as this thread documents , nearly every relevant local ballot measure opposing data centers won or is winning ( the only exception so far was in North Dakota ) — is that the constraint on AI dispersion has shifted once again. First we were short on compute, but that ramped; now we are short on memory, but that will ramp; we were coming close to being short on power, but that will be rectified. The final constraint is political, and that may be the most imposing constraint of all. Not only is it harder to solve, but it actually interferes with solving the other constraints. Many of the theories about AI assume that it becomes a commodity; I think it’s just as likely we are looking at scarcity for much longer than we expected, which will have ripple effects on everything.

 Ten Takes

 To that end, here — with the caveat that nothing leads to hot takes you regret like an election — are ten perspectives on what a permanently impaired ability to build might mean. To be clear, I’m not declaring permanency — look at how our elections swing back and forth — but it’s worth considering what the implications might be if Americans don’t change their minds about data centers.

 1. The AI Trade Got It Right

 The most obvious reason why the stock market has been rocky over the last few weeks is the tightening of credit markets, which I wrote about this summer . We are, needless to say, full on into the equity funding era (and while I’m here, I haven’t written about Anthropic’s updated S-1 , but it strongly affirms my initial analysis ). At the same time, it seems clear that this outcome is very bad for the AI trade in the short term, but much of the pain may have already been endured.

 2. Neoclouds on the Edge

 The Neoclouds have been at the forefront of credit concerns, and from a certain perspective, being unable to build data centers has a silver lining in that they couldn’t get the money to pay for them anyways. Moreover, Neoclouds with facilities that are already permitted now have an asset that is going to be scarcer than expected. At the same time, it’s Neoclouds that need new sites and new permits, even as they are likely to have much less political sway than the hyperscalers — who already have more sites they can repurpose or rebuild. It was already getting harder to get capital, relative to the hyperscalers; now you have to layer on that it’s going to be harder to get permission, too.

 3. Hyperscalers Are Winners

 The downside for the neoclouds is upside for the hyperscalers, who are more likely to grow their share of AI compute than they were before. Moreover, investors may be pleased if the hyperscalers’ ambitions are somewhat curtailed; political opposition is an excuse to moderate spending, knowing that everyone else is in the same boat.

 4. Nvidia’s Mixed Bag

 Nvidia will almost certainly be a short-term loser. Fewer data centers mean fewer Nvidia chips generally, and a weakened Neocloud set is particularly harmful not only because Neoclouds almost exclusively use Nvidia full-rack systems, but also because Nvidia is back-stopping a huge number of them. It’s the hyperscalers, meanwhile, who are Nvidia’s biggest long-term threat, given their scale and ability to invest in their own chips.

 At the same time, a constrained world makes Nvidia’s offerings more compelling. CEO Jensen Huang actually spent an entire keynote making this point back in 2025; I wrote in an Update :

 When Huang says “iso power” he means that power is the constraint; the question is how many tokens can you generate given a fixed power envelope, and Blackwell can generate a lot more. These were the numbers Huang gave for a 100 MW data center:

 What this means is that the first order of business for an ASIC maker is to match that level of efficiency. That, though, means keeping up with Nvidia’s product development cadence; The Information has a post about Amazon offering instances using its latest Trainium ASIC at a significant discount to the H100. Huang, though, spent this keynote insulting the H100! You can almost hear him speaking to Amazon directly: you spent all this money, and are offering these huge discounts, just to entice developers to lock themselves into an inferior chip, even as reasoning models are going to swamp your available power generation…

 Huang is issuing a challenge to every cloud provider tempted to make an ASIC: do you really think that you can keep up with this, and risk running out of power capacity because your chips aren’t efficient enough? Don’t even try.

 A world without power or data center constraints is one where it is, in the very long run, very difficult to maintain Nvidia’s margins; once those constraints start to bite, however, an advantage in tokens/megawatt is worth a lot of money. Go back to my point about the hyperscalers: one way to generate more tokens is to build a new data center; another way is to rebuild a data center with new Nvidia chips.

 5. Advantage China

 China is the inverse of the scenario that Huang laid out: the country has plenty of power and the ability to build a lot more, but they don’t have leading-edge chips. Some of the advantages of leading-edge chips, however, can be overcome by simply throwing tons of electricity at the problem. From a 2025 Update about the Huawei CloudMatrix 384 supercomputer:

 The CloudMatrix 384, which is a supercomputer consisting of 384 chips, takes up dramatically more space, uses dramatically more power, is almost certainly dramatically more expensive to make, and is dramatically more brittle than Nvidia’s NVL72; there is no one in the world who would choose the CloudMatrix 384 over the NVL72 if they had the choice.

 That’s the thing, though: China doesn’t have the choice, because of U.S. export controls. The country’s saving grace is that they are operating on different constraints than the U.S.…China — which actually builds power generation — is not iso power; they are iso compute: Huawei’s goal with the CloudMatrix 384 is to get as much compute as possible, power efficiency be damned.

 In the fullness of time — i.e. as China figures out leading-edge chips — this may be an insurmountable advantage.

 6. Data Centers in Space

 When SpaceX released their S-1, I explicitly pointed to political opposition to data centers as one of the company’s most significant upside scenarios:

 The third question about data centers in space is if there is a stick. Specifically, while I think that racks-in-space are both a lot more viable than people think, and a lot more relevant to agentic inference than current modes of compute, it is at the end of the day cheaper and easier to build on earth, all things being equal.

 All things are not equal, however: right now we are at the very beginning of the AI buildout and already one of the biggest constraints is not just power (expected), but zoning (unexpected). I wrote in an Update last week:

 I already posted the relevant excerpt above. Continuing:

 In that Update I made the case that data center builders — and by extension the companies that use them — should straight up pay people for permission to build data centers in their communities. At a minimum, however, that increases the costs of terrestrial data centers. What seems very plausible in the long run is that the demand for compute ends up being so large that there event...

Read Online | Sign Up | Advertise

 Good morning, {{ first_name | AI enthusiasts }}, and welcome to our 4,926 new readers. Years of Apple Intelligence and one full Siri rebuild later, the iPhone still doesn’t feel any more like a device built for the AI era. Could letting other apps in finally change that?
 Apple just opened up building on its Siri AI to all developers, something the notoriously closed-off ecosystem rarely allows. But none of it reaches the App Store until spring, which could be a whole different AI era for a product already feeling generations behind.
 Founders and solo operators: You’re doing the work of a whole team by yourself — show us how AI makes that possible. Outreach, invoicing, content, customer replies, anything counts. Submit your workflow for a chance to be featured in the newsletter.

---
 In today’s AI rundown:
 Apple lets any app plug into Siri AI

 Google won’t give schools Search without AI

 Turn one product photo into three studio shots

 CrowdStrike’s ‘kill switch’ to stop rogue AI agents

 LATEST DEVELOPMENTS

 APPLE
 🍎  Apple lets any app plug into Siri AI
 Image source: Apple

 The Rundown: Apple just released a developer preview of Siri AI in its latest software betas, giving apps of any kind a way to build their own features into the assistant — though developers can only test it for now, and customers are still months away.
 The details:
 Siri AI is Apple’s rebuilt assistant, able to see a user’s screen and read messages, and has been a waitlisted beta since iOS 27 shipped in September.

 Developers can now add their own actions instead of just Apple’s initial preset list of options, and teach Siri multi-step jobs through new “skills.”

 For now, app versions stay with a developer’s internal testers, App Store submissions start in spring, and Apple says rules for developers will come later.

 The betas also bring China its first Apple Intelligence tools (minus Siri AI) and test new Apple Watch tools that listen in the background to transcribe nearby talk.

 Why it matters: Apple letting any app build into Siri is a real crack in its walled garden, which is a big deal. Still, it leaves the work on developers, and between Siri AI’s confusing rollout and the progress other frontier labs have made in areas like computer use, the best AI features still feel a long way off for the world’s most popular phone.

 TOGETHER WITH WIZ
 🔒 Securing AI Agents 101

 The Rundown: AI agents are rapidly emerging across enterprise environments: powering automation, chaining tools, and acting across systems. Securing AI Agents 101 is a one-page resource to help teams build a clear understanding of what AI agents are, how they operate, and where key security considerations show up.
 Inside, you’ll find:
 What makes an AI agent different from traditional tools

 Top risks to watch, from shadow AI to excessive permissions

 Four key questions to assess agent usage and exposure

 Get the one-page guide to AI agents .

 GOOGLE & AI IN SCHOOLS
 🏫  Google won’t give schools Search without AI
 Image source: Google

 The Rundown: Google announced that K-12 student accounts will start with Search, Gemini, and Gemini Notebook all off early next year, potentially forcing districts that want AI out of classrooms to also give up Google Search for their students.
 The details:
 Education VP Chris Phillips said to The New York Times that “Search and A.I. are deeply integrated,” and students at AI-free schools will see a notice that it’s off.

 NYC and LA, the two largest U.S. districts, restricted AI for ~1M students this semester, and Fairfax County, VA, built a plugin to hide Google’s AI summaries.

 Google’s announcement also comes one day after the Nov. 2 deadline senators gave the company to answer questions about pushing AI into schools.

 Ex-FTC Chair Lina Khan said Google is using “its search monopoly to coerce schools” and will “punish those who don’t fall in line.”

 Google later defended the move on X as “more choice, not less,” but its post only describes Search with AI Mode and AI Overviews, never without them.

 Why it matters: Google is essentially saying out loud what the trend has shown — Google Search is AI search now — and schools aren’t getting the old version back. The stranger situation will be AI-free districts with kids on Chromebooks, turning in work through Classroom, and writing in Docs, yet unable to use Search.

 AI TRAINING
 📷  Turn one product photo into three studio shots

 The Rundown: In this guide, you’ll build a product-shoot app in Runway using an image of a vintage Polaroid camera. You’ll create coral, sunlit, and blue-lit scenes, then save the app so you can repeat the process.
 Step-by-step:
 Save the guide’s Polaroid photo and its credit. Open Runway App Studio and check that your plan and credit balance support a build

 Paste the build prompt to create an app with three shoot presets. Check the product upload, scene menu, and download controls before running it

 Upload the original photo and list the camera details to preserve. Make one coral studio shot and inspect the lens, rainbow stripe, buttons, and lettering

 Run the same photo through the sunlit and blue-lit presets. Keep the camera’s shape and viewpoint consistent, and save each approved result

 Publish the app for yourself, then open all three downloads. Keep the source credit and a record of any defects with the set

 Pro tip: Use the original product photo for every scene. Starting from a flawed AI image can carry its mistakes into the next shot. Visit The Rundown University to get the full guide, materials, files, and more.

 PRESENTED BY PITCH
 📣  Teams riding the AI wave present with Pitch

 The Rundown: The teams building AI make their slides with Pitch. It’s how Perplexity, fal, Legora, Poolside, and Synthesia create and deliver presentations at scale.
 Pitch is an agentic presentation platform where you can:
 Generate fully editable decks from your own templates, so every slide stays on brand

 Connect via MCP to personalize slides with data from your CRM or call notes

 Nurture deals with custom pitch rooms, and track how buyers engage with built-in analytics

 Try Pitch .

 CROWDSTRIKE & AI SECURITY
 🛑  CrowdStrike’s ‘kill switch’ to stop rogue AI agents
 Image source: CrowdStrike

 The Rundown: Cybersecurity firm CrowdStrike unveiled the AI Kill Switch, adding an emergency stop to its Falcon Guardian security platform for businesses worried about their AI agents going rogue.
 The details:
 The switch targets an agent’s link to its AI model, not the model itself, while Falcon Guardian separately monitors tools like Claude Code and Codex.

 A human admin has to pull the trigger, and every use gets logged, while shutting agents down directly on work devices and in the cloud is “coming soon.”

 CEO George Kurtz explained it like a race car’s brake, saying it sits outside the AI so an agent “can’t argue with it, rewrite it, or wait it out.”

 CrowdStrike is also buying monitoring firm Fiddler AI and security tester Dreadnode for a reported $495M, and added Claude Cowork protection in beta.

 Why it matters: Politicians have spent the summer fighting over an AI kill switch, with a pair of bills and a California executive order aimed at rogue AI agents. CrowdStrike is bringing the same concept to enterprises… where the likelier scenario isn’t a frontier model escaping a lab, but an agent holding the company’s logins going off script.

 QUICK HITS

 COMMUNITY AI WORKFLOW OF THE DAY
 ▸ Erin built a self-drafting timesheet with Claude
 Today’s workflow comes from reader Erin Reid :
 “Late timesheets delayed accurate client billing for our advertising and marketing agency, so I built a Claude project that reconstructs my week from the tools I already use. It drafts time entries that I review and approve before anything reaches our system. It’s useful for anyone who logs time after the fact and loses track of smaller tasks.
 It searches the emails I sent or replied to, my calendar meetings, files I edited in Google Drive, Slack threads I joined, work-related browsing, and Claude work sessions. It builds a daily timeline and groups related items into one block. An email, a doc edit, and a Slack thread about the same issue count once.
 The project instructions require Claude never to invent work or pad hours, never to double-count, and to disclose any source it couldn’t search. Instead of trying to remember my week, I now review entries that already have project codes and descriptions, and it also surfaces work I had forgotten.”

blogs.name: Tomasz Tunguz
blogs.title: Watts in Store for 2027 : The AI Ceiling
blogs.description: The ceiling for AI in 2027 is about 80gw : doubling all the compute built in the history of the country in twelve months. Yet even at this…
blogs.content:
The ceiling for AI in 2027 is about 80gw : doubling all the compute built in the history of the country in twelve months.

 Yet even at this historic pace, the hourly cost of GPUs has doubled in the last six months : short-term rental rates have jumped from $3 to $12-13 per hour, pushing Anthropic’s blended GPU-hour cost up 82% in just two quarters. 1 Finished server racks are already sitting unpowered in staging warehouses because data centers lack the energized utility power to turn them on.

 When supply doubles & prices still double, demand is fundamentally outrunning physical reality. There will consistently be an active ceiling on energized compute, which will keep structural upward pressure on GPU prices per hour.

 On last night’s All-In election livestream, Brad Gerstner framed that buildout in gigawatts :

 “The consensus forecast is a total of 43 gigawatts coming online in 2027… the total gigawatts online at the end of ‘26, the cumulative in the United States, is about 38 … I think we could see at least 10 to 15 gigawatts of the expected build not come online.” 2

 What does a ceiling like this mean for AI?

 First, there’s a theoretical maximum amount of revenue we can generate from AI. A GPU can perform two types of tasks for AI : inference & training. Today, 40% of GPU hours are inference : AI sold to customers. 3 The other 60% develops models.

 Today’s 38gw fleet earns about $140b, while the 43gw to be added in 2027 will run on chips that are 3-5x more powerful & should deliver an annualized earnings capability of about $350b, for a total of nearly $500b. 4

 As GPU prices continue to rise, foundation model companies may need to shift the fraction of GPU hours to inference from training. This might limit the pace of innovation at the frontier.

 Second, latency becomes the release valve for too much demand. Internet access is priced in terms of bandwidth (gigabytes of files you can download) & speed (how quickly you can download it). AI may be priced the same way. We see this already with products focused on low-latency inference & those on long-horizon tasks. 5

 Third, limitations in compute availability will encourage algorithmic innovation. Chinese models like DeepSeek, Qwen, & Kimi have demonstrated material architectural advantages that drive near-state-of-the-art performance on much smaller models & new architectures. 6

 Fourth, the harness becomes critical to deliver state-of-the-art performance on limited GPU availability. Responsible for more than half of system performance, the software around the model can extract tremendous efficiency. 7

 Fifth, the economics of vibe-coding face a reality check. When inference becomes more expensive, off-the-shelf software (with AI) can be less expensive than bespoke built & maintained internal software.

 In 2027, AI’s constraint will be access to powered GPUs. As the prices for renting GPUs continues to increase faster than efficiency can fight, watts in store for 2027? Efficiency as the dominant motif up & down the stack.

blogs.title: Apple Earnings, Memory Problems, The Hardware Company Regression
blogs.author: Ben Thompson
blogs.description: Apple's earnings suggest that the company's hardware business is doing better than ever, even in the face of memory challenges. Does the software story help or hurt?
blogs.content:
Apple's earnings suggest that the company's hardware business is doing better than ever, even in the face of memory challenges. Does the software story help or hurt?

---

Listen to this Update in your podcast player

---

Good morning,

Over on Asianometry , Jon explains The Rise of GLM and China’s Zhipu AI , and also gives a trip report from Silicon Valley .

On to the Update:

Apple Earnings

From the Wall Street Journal :

The Apple growth and profit machine is wavering, and the boost from price increases might not be enough to keep it going at historic rates. That dials up the pressure on Apple’s new chief executive, John Ternus. The company saved the bad news for its earnings call, an hour after it posted its results for the September quarter, projecting that for the current quarter its high-margin services business will continue to slow and that its widely watched gross profit margin will continue to fall.

Apple shares had been flat in post-close trading but declined as much as 4% after the company made the projections, which fell short of Wall Street estimates. The impact of high memory costs are weighing even more heavily on the company, Ternus and Apple Chief Financial Officer Kevan Parekh said on the company’s earnings call. Apple has stockpiled cheaper components purchased earlier, but those inventories are dwindling…

Investors have bid up Apple shares because it has been a port in the AI storm—a reliable and capital-efficient business that stands apart from rivals which are spending hundreds of billions of dollars racing to the AI frontier. While others invest in data centers, Apple has been pouring its own cash into buybacks and dividends. But that safety may be challenged if Ternus can’t speed up Apple’s innovation engine.

Actually, I thought that on his maiden earnings call Ternus made a good case that Apple’s innovation engine is running pretty well:

This is an amazing time at Apple. We just completed one of the most prolific launch periods in our history. It’s been a remarkable time for innovation across all of our categories. One of the greatest testaments to that is the all-new iPhone Duo, the most transformational iPhone since the original. We’re also incredibly excited about iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max, which take massive leaps forward on camera, battery life, and performance—features that our users care deeply about. Meanwhile, touch has arrived on Mac for the first time with the all-new MacBook Pro. And we were excited to announce the new iMac and 14-inch MacBook Pro. The all-new iPad mini features a stunning new OLED display and brings a super thin design to the smallest member of the iPad family. Apple Watch now offers users the clearest window yet into their heart health. We introduced AirPods 5, which feature industry-leading active noise cancellation in an open-ear design. And we’ve laid the foundation for an even more intelligent smart home with the all-new HomeView, Apple TV 4K, and HomePod mini.

That’s a lot of new products, and the headliner — the iPhone Duo — appears to be a big hit, murmurs about hinge issues notwithstanding. Speaking anecdotally, the response to the device amongst normal users is extremely positive, even if it doesn’t appeal to more hardcore users ; to the extent that is true, that’s a positive sign, in two regards: first, it’s a pleasant reminder that people who obsess over this stuff don’t always represent normal users, and second, there is still room for Apple to segment the market, not just by price but also through fundamental design (as for me, I’m waiting for the Air 2).

Meanwhile, the new MacBook Pro with touch is exactly the computer I’ve been hoping for ever since I first used computers with touch displays at Microsoft 15 years ago. What Microsoft got wrong with Windows 8 was that they overhauled the interface to be touch-first; yes, you can use a mouse-and-keyboard with a touch interface easily enough, but it’s too easy: you give up a lot of power and control in exchange for denominating the user interface by the least precise input method.

Apple didn’t do that: touch is just an extra interaction layer that is there when you need it, and not catered to when you don’t; that’s exactly where Microsoft ended up too, which is why nearly all high-end Windows devices still have touch, even if the operating system long ago reverted towards being built around precise mouse-and-keyboard interfaces. This isn’t a touch-screen computer; it’s a computer that you can touch when and if you find it convenient (and having used them, it’s very nice to have!).

---

Presented by

I spend a lot of time trying to figure out what is happening to businesses on the internet. Luckily, our new advertising partner Stripe has the unique position of processing the equivalent of 1.7% of global GDP, making it, in a sense, a barometer of the economy.

Their latest SaaS data , for example, shows that while SaaS stocks were supposedly experiencing an apocalypse, revenue growth was actually accelerating. You can read about that disconnect on their Stripe Economics blog on Substack.

I suspect there’s a lot more hiding in Stripe’s data and I’m looking forward to having an excuse to dig into it.

---

Memory Problems

Apple first started pushing the narrative that they were a services company in 2016, but, as I argued at the time , that was more aspirational and narrative selling than reality, given the fact the stock market was still focused on iPhone sales; three years later, however, when Apple stopped reporting unit sales and started talking about its installed base I called the switch: Apple was a services company . Three years after that, I was shocked when the company didn’t raise prices in the face of inflation , but I shouldn’t have been: effectively lowering prices — which helps gain market share — is exactly the right approach to take if growing services is the top priority. Indeed, Apple continued to not (or barely) raise prices for years after that, and then came the memory crisis.

It was memory that dominated the Q&A on the earnings call, and it’s hitting Apple on multiple fronts. First, even with June’s price increases (which didn’t include the iPhone), margins were down by about one percentage point because of memory. Second, even with price increases both in September (on the iPhone) and October (on Macs and iPads, above and beyond the summer’s increase), margins will decrease by another 1.5–2 percentage points. Moreover, Ternus said it’s going to get worse:

Let me give you an overall view on memory. What we’re seeing with memory pricing right now is unprecedented, and as we said earlier in the September quarter, we did see higher memory costs as compared to the June quarter, which were partly offset by the benefit of carry-in inventory and lower costs on certain non-memory components. Now, for the December quarter, we expect even higher memory costs, partly offset by a few factors. So, as we said, we changed the price on many of our products, including Mac and iPad at the end of June, and iPhone in September, and these price increases provided some offset. We also expect to see some benefit from carry-in inventory in the December quarter as well, as well as lower costs on certain non-memory components. And looking beyond the December quarter, we see the pricing for memory purchases continuing to increase. As we said before, we do believe we will see a decreasing benefit from the carry-in inventory on memory over time. And there is one more thing I wanted to add. As we work to improve supply, our manufacturing purchase obligations have increased by $33 billion from June to the September quarter, which you’ll see in our annual filing when it comes out tomorrow. Now back to Kevan for the other parts of it.

That last bit is point number three: Apple is having to make significant purchase obligations to secure memory, likely locking in these high prices. Fourth, despite those purchase obligations — or perhaps because purchase obligations are necessary — Apple actually doesn’t have enough memory! This was COO Sabih Khan, the second new addition to the earnings call:

So during the September quarter, we experienced supply constraints on iPhone, Mac and iPad, and this was driven by the high levels of demand, and as we’ve said before, we’re seeing less flexibility in the supply chain than normal. The Q4 constraints were primarily driven by the availability of the advanced nodes our SOCs are produced on, but as we have transitioned more of our lineup to the latest 2nm technology nodes, our constraints on advanced nodes are easing. And for the December quarter, we expect constraints on Mac and iPad, primarily driven by memory, as demand has been higher than what we expected.

I made this point previously in the context of those SoC constraints, which is that Apple isn’t just used to dictating price to suppliers, but also having the freedom to ramp its manufacturing up and down in response to demand while forcing those suppliers to maintain the capacity and inventory to meet their needs. Now, however, Apple has to actually forecast demand, knowing that if they forecast too low they won’t sell as much as they could have, and if they forecast too high they are the ones who have to carry excess inventory.

The Hardware Company Regression

The good news for Apple goes back to the innovation question: the company is consistently missing its forecasts by underestimating demand. Of course it would be ideal if the company had enough devices to sell to everyone who wanted one, as soon as they want it, but in the grand scheme of things it’s good news that Apple devices seem to be more popular than ever. Moreover, that popularity is increasing even as the price increases. CFO Kevan Parekh was, understandably, unwilling to say this was a trend:

If I kind of unpack the comments around supply chain, about availability of components, and your outlook for the December quarter, can you help us understand sort of the difference or maybe the delta of quantity versus price across the product lineup? Because it certainly looks like you’re looking at double digit growth across the iPhone and the Mac business, and we all know, I think, in the industry that there’s been pretty strong price inflation across the PC/Mac ecosystem, and you guys mentioned that you’ve reluctantly taken price as well. So can you help us understand kind of what’s the driving dynamics in that market?

KP : We don’t normally provide that level of detail or color as we look at the outlook, other than to say, again, we did guide to the 7% to 10% year on year, and again, just as a reminder, that is on top of a phenomenal December quarter last year, where revenue grew 16%, and so we don’t provide the level of detail, but I would say it’s early to really read price elasticity at this point in time. The iPad and Mac were constrained since we had made those adjustments, and again, we just recently just adjusted the price on iPhone, so it’s really early to really assess any elasticity impact at this stage.

This explains why I was so shocked when Apple didn’t raise prices four years ago; from the very beginning of Stratechery I’ve been wondering just how high Apple could raise prices without significantly hurting demand, and well, the seeming answer — just as it was with the iPhone 5S vs 5C, and just as it was with the iPhone X — is significantly higher!

There is, however, one fly in the ointment; this was the paragraph that came after Ternus’ opening extolling Apple’s hardware launches:

On top of it all, we’re unlocking more powerful AI experiences across our lineup, including with the all-new Siri AI, a profoundly capable and deeply personal assistant seamlessly integrated across our platforms. And like everything we make, Siri AI is built with essential privacy protections so no one can access users’ data, not even Apple. We launched Siri AI in beta for US English users in Septem...
